excel.w: Connects everyday work to adidas’ purpose, products, consumers, and culture — in actions, not just words.
excel.a: Do I feel more connected to adidas because of how the people around me show up?

excel.w: Takes real ownership of outcomes, balancing impact on people and the business.
excel.a: Do I take ownership for outcomes even when it’s uncomfortable, even without a title?

excel.w: Looks ahead, challenges the way things are usually done, and makes room for better solutions.
excel.a: Am I helping the team look ahead, or only reacting to what’s in front of us?

scored.inclusion: Helps create an environment where different perspectives are genuinely valued and included.
scored.engage: Brings energy and clarity that helps the people around you do their best work.
scored.develop: Actively supports a colleague’s growth through honest, specific feedback.
scored.results: Helps turn good ideas into outcomes by making space for them to be heard.
scored.accountability: Names issues constructively instead of letting them slide, even without formal authority.
scored.grow: Stays open to feedback and curious about your own blind spots.

phases.title: You Were In the Room
narrative: You’re not the manager. But you were in the meeting when Mike laughed off Alex’s idea — “we actually tried that years ago, I guess every new hire has to rediscover our old mistakes” — and you saw Alex go quiet for the rest of the meeting.
No one else seems to have noticed, or maybe they noticed and decided not to act. You don’t have a leadership title here — but it’s clear this landed on Alex.
You have a short window, still inside the meeting, to decide if you do anything.

choices.l: Support Alex’s idea right there, without confronting Mike directly
choices.t: “Actually, I think there’s something here — Alex, can you say more about how this would’ve helped with last month’s issue?”
choices.imm: The conversation returns to Alex’s idea, without naming Mike’s comment. Alex seems a little more at ease continuing.
choices.del: Alex remembers that someone pulled the idea back to the table — but Mike’s comment itself was never named by anyone.
choices.why: This gives Alex space back without turning the meeting into a confrontation that isn’t yours to lead — a real way to act without formal authority. The cost is that the pattern itself stays unnamed, and stays easier to repeat.

choices.l: Stay quiet in the meeting, but check in with Alex privately afterward
choices.t: You say nothing in the moment. Later, you message Alex: “Saw what happened earlier. Your idea made sense to me.”
choices.imm: Alex replies with a brief but genuine-sounding “thanks.”
choices.del: Alex knows at least one person noticed. But no one in the room saw it happen, so the group’s norm doesn’t shift.
choices.why: A private show of support is real and low-risk — a solid first step if you don’t want to put Alex further in the spotlight. The cost is that it’s invisible to the rest of the team, who still don’t know that comment bothered anyone.

choices.l: Assume the manager will notice and handle it — not your role to fix
choices.t: You figure that stepping in isn’t your place; your manager is in the room and can notice on their own.
choices.imm: The meeting continues. No one else comments.
choices.del: Weeks later, you notice Alex barely speaks up in meetings anymore — and you can’t say whether anyone, including you, ever did anything about it.
choices.why: It’s true that publicly correcting a colleague isn’t the job of whoever doesn’t run the meeting — that hesitation is reasonable. But psychological safety doesn’t depend only on who has a title: waiting for someone else is also a choice, and it has a cost.

phases.title: Mike Interrupts Again
narrative: Two weeks later, Mike cuts Alex off mid-explanation — again. His suggestion isn’t even wrong, but it’s the second time this month. Your manager is in the meeting and doesn’t react.
You’re Alex’s peer, not Mike’s manager. Still, what you do in the next few seconds shapes what the room learns is normal.

choices.l: Step in, lightly, as a peer
choices.t: “Hold on, let Alex finish — I think there’s more there.”
choices.imm: Mike stops. “My bad,” he says. Alex finishes the point.
choices.del: Alex notices that someone other than the manager noticed and acted. Mike is slightly more careful around you too, afterward.
choices.why: A peer stepping in, not just the manager, sends a strong signal that this doesn’t depend only on who has a title. The risk is that it can look like you’re publicly correcting a senior colleague, which not everyone in the room may read well.

choices.l: Let it pass, but check with Alex about whether they want support raising it with the manager
choices.t: After the meeting: “I noticed Mike cut you off again. Want me to mention it to our manager with you, or would you rather handle it your own way?”
choices.imm: Alex is relieved someone noticed, but hesitates: “I don’t know if I want to make this a whole thing.”
choices.del: The decision correctly stays with Alex — but the pattern keeps happening while they decide.
choices.why: Asking Alex, instead of deciding for them, respects the autonomy of the person most affected — exactly the kind of support any peer can offer. The cost is that a solution may take longer while the pattern keeps repeating.

choices.l: Message the manager directly about it, without talking to Alex first
choices.t: After the meeting you write to the manager: “Noticed Mike cut Alex off again, thought you should know.”
choices.imm: The manager thanks you for the flag. Alex doesn’t know this conversation happened.
choices.del: If Alex finds out later, they may feel their situation became someone else’s topic without being consulted — even with good intent on your part.
choices.why: Flagging it to the manager is a legitimate move and can speed up a real correction. The cost is deciding this without including Alex, who arguably has the most say in how and when their own situation gets raised.

phases.title: Telling Mike Yourself
narrative: You decide the pattern is clear enough that Mike should hear it directly from a peer, not just from a manager. You’re weighing tone and setting — something fair, respectful, and that actually gets through.
Every option you’re considering has a catch, even though none of them look outright wrong.

choices.l: Post a general reminder in the team channel, without naming him
choices.t: “Friendly reminder: let’s all make sure we let people finish their thoughts before jumping in — goes for all of us :)” you post in the team channel.
choices.imm: A few people react with a thumbs up. Mike doesn’t respond at all.
choices.del: Because it was addressed to everyone, Mike can reasonably assume it wasn’t about him — and the specific pattern with Alex goes unaddressed.
choices.why: A public, general reminder avoids singling anyone out, which can feel like the fairer, lower-risk option. The cost is that vague, addressed-to-everyone feedback lets the one person it’s actually about opt out of hearing it — and it does nothing for Alex, who watched it happen and knows exactly who it was about.

choices.l: Tell him “a few people have noticed,” without saying who
choices.t: “Hey, a few people have noticed you cutting folks off in meetings — might be worth watching.”
choices.imm: Mike looks caught off guard. “Who said that?” he asks. You don’t answer.
choices.del: Mike spends the next few days wondering who’s talking about him behind his back, more focused on that than on the actual behavior.
choices.why: Citing “a few people” can feel like it adds weight, and protects any one person from being identified as the source. But invoking an anonymous collective makes the feedback feel like it’s coming from everywhere and nowhere — it’s hard for Mike to actually engage with, and can read as being ganged up on rather than given honest, ownable feedback.

choices.l: Bring it up casually at the team happy hour, so it feels lower-stakes
choices.t: At drinks after work, you mention it lightly: “Haha, you really shut Alex down earlier, huh?”
choices.imm: Mike laughs it off in the moment: “Yeah, yeah, my bad.” The conversation moves on immediately.
choices.del: Because it was framed as a joke in a social setting, Mike doesn’t register it as feedback at all — and nothing changes.
choices.why: A casual, social moment can feel like the least confrontational way to raise something, and sometimes lands better than a formal sit-down. The cost is that wrapping real feedback in a joke, in a space that’s implicitly off-duty, makes it easy for the other person not to take it seriously — and mixes a corrective conversation into a space that’s supposed to be free of exactly that.

phases.title: Trying to Help
narrative: You finally decide to talk to Alex about all of this. Your intentions are good — but the three easiest ways to open this conversation share one problem, even though none of them looks wrong at first glance.

choices.t: “Don’t worry about it, Mike’s like that with everyone, it’s not personal.”
choices.imm: Alex nods, but doesn’t seem more relieved — just ready to drop the subject.
choices.del: Alex learns that raising this again will likely be met with “it’s not a big deal” — which discourages them from bringing it up if it happens again.
choices.why: This feels comforting and tries to lighten the moment — a genuine intention. But minimizing invalidates Alex’s experience before you’ve even really heard it — deciding it’s “not personal” isn’t your call to make for them.

choices.l: Center a similar experience of your own
choices.t: “Oh, I know exactly how that feels, he does that to me too, this one time...” — and you keep going with your own story.
choices.imm: Alex listens politely, but barely gets to return to their own point.
choices.del: Alex leaves the conversation feeling like they came to vent and ended up hearing about someone else’s experience.
choices.why: Sharing a similar experience can genuinely build connection and show Alex they’re not alone. The problem is when it takes over the space — Alex’s psychological safety depends on being heard, not on you feeling understood.

choices.l: Offer to fix it for them, without asking first
choices.t: “Leave it with me, I’ll talk to Mike about this directly.”
choices.imm: Alex says “okay,” a little uncertain, without having asked for this.
choices.del: If the conversation with Mike doesn’t go well, Alex may end up in the middle of a tension they didn’t choose — and without being consulted on how they wanted their own situation handled.
choices.why: Offering to take concrete action comes from real care, and is sometimes exactly what someone wants. The problem is assuming that without asking — it takes away Alex’s choice over whether and how their situation gets addressed by someone else.

phases.title: When (and How) to Escalate
narrative: The pattern with Mike continues, week after week. Alex still hasn’t formally raised it. You notice it’s also costing the team — good ideas aren’t reaching the table, and some technical calls are slower or worse without Alex’s input.
There’s more than one reasonable way to take this forward — and each comes with a different cost.

choices.l: Raise it now, with what you’ve seen, even without Alex asking
choices.t: You set up time with your manager and describe the pattern you’ve observed, being clear it’s your own read, not Alex’s.
choices.imm: The manager thanks you and says they’ll pay closer attention.
choices.del: Something shifts faster — but Alex may feel surprised to learn their situation was raised without them choosing the timing.
choices.why: Acting on what you’ve seen, and being transparent that it’s your own read, is a legitimate way to keep a real pattern from waiting too long — and it connects directly to the quality of the team’s decisions. The cost is deciding the timing for Alex, even with good intent.

choices.l: Wait for an even clearer pattern before taking it anywhere
choices.t: You decide you’re still not certain enough, and prefer to keep watching a while longer.
choices.imm: Nothing changes in the short term.
choices.del: The pattern repeats once more, in a similar way, before anything is said.
choices.why: Wanting certainty before acting is a genuine form of care and avoids false alarms. The risk is that you’ve already seen this pattern repeat more than once — waiting for “even clearer” can become a way of postponing indefinitely.

choices.l: Use an indirect channel — an engagement survey or anonymous feedback tool
choices.t: You log what you observed in the company’s anonymous feedback channel, without naming specific people.
choices.imm: It gets recorded, without directly exposing anyone.
choices.del: It may take longer to turn into concrete action, and it’s unclear whether anyone will connect that entry to Alex’s situation.
choices.why: An indirect channel is a real tool when a direct conversation feels too risky, and it doesn’t require anyone to expose themselves. The cost is speed, and the chance the signal gets lost among other entries.

champion.name: Consistent Psychological Safety Ally
champion.sum: Even without a leadership title, you acted consistently, respectfully, and specifically — protecting space for whoever had less power in the room, even when it wasn’t technically your job.
champion.str: Notices patterns early. Acts with care for the other person’s autonomy. Doesn’t wait passively for whoever has the title.
champion.risk: Watch out for taking on the role of “fixing it” for others — ask before acting on someone’s behalf.

inconsistent.name: Well-Meaning but Inconsistent Peer
inconsistent.sum: You care, but your responses varied — sometimes real, careful support, other times avoidance or making the moment about you.
inconsistent.risk: Inconsistency can be confusing for someone who needs predictable, not occasional, support.

avoider.name: Cautious Bystander
avoider.sum: You tend to wait for formal leadership to fix things, even when you sense something is wrong. That’s understandable — it’s not your title — but it has a real cost for whoever is affected.
avoider.risk: Silence can read as agreement, even without meaning to.

silencer.name: Unintended Reinforcer
silencer.sum: Your choices — minimizing, centering yourself, acting without asking — likely made it harder, without meaning to, for Alex to feel truly heard. This is common among well-intentioned colleagues.
silencer.risk: Good intentions don’t guarantee the affected person feels supported.

CONT.inclusion: Handing the floor back to quieter colleagues when you notice space closing.
CONT.engage: Bringing lightness and trust into tense moments between colleagues.
CONT.develop: Offering specific, not just generic, support to whoever needs it.
CONT.results: Noticing when a colleague’s silence may be costing the team quality.
CONT.accountability: Naming patterns, even without a title, instead of waiting for whoever has one.
CONT.grow: Asking before acting on someone else’s behalf.

START.inclusion: Actively inviting quieter colleagues back into the conversation.
START.engage: Using tension as a chance for connection, not just discomfort to avoid.
START.develop: Offering concrete support by asking what the person actually needs.
START.results: Connecting your support to better technical calls for the team.
START.accountability: Raising repeated patterns, even when it’s not formally your role.
START.grow: Asking a trusted colleague whether your way of helping actually helps.

COMMIT.inclusion: In the next meeting, I will notice who went quiet and bring them back into the conversation.
COMMIT.engage: Next time a colleague goes through something hard, I will ask how to support before acting.
COMMIT.develop: This week, I will offer one piece of specific, not generic, support to a colleague.
COMMIT.results: This week, I will notice whether any silence on the team may be costing us a better decision.
COMMIT.accountability: This week, I will name one pattern I’ve been letting slide, even if it’s not formally my role.
COMMIT.grow: This month, I will ask a colleague whether my way of supporting them actually helps.

DISC.inclusion: What concrete habit would help a quieter colleague feel invited to speak up?
DISC.engage: How do you tell the difference between supporting someone and centering the conversation on yourself?
DISC.develop: How could you practice asking “how can I help” before acting on someone’s behalf?
DISC.results: What decision on your team could have been better if someone had felt safe to speak up earlier?
DISC.accountability: What pattern between colleagues have you been letting slide because it’s not “formally your job”?
DISC.grow: Who could you ask whether your way of supporting people is actually useful?
